title: The Deschamps paradox: was his World Cup-winning Les Bleus tenure a success?
content:
Dynasties rarely end with a bang. More often, they fade quietly, leaving only numbers and memories to tell the story.
Didier Deschamps departs the France dugout after 187 matches in charge, having won 122 of them, drawn 32 and lost only 33 — a remarkable 65.2% win rate. But statistics alone cannot explain his tenure.
He inherited a national team weighed down by embarrassment and disappointment when he succeeded Laurent Blanc in 2012. The side was still scarred by one of the darkest episodes in its footballing history. The disastrous 2010 World Cup campaign in South Africa had descended into chaos, culminating in the players’ infamous ‘mutiny’ against erstwhile manager Raymond Domenech. Blanc’s subsequent two-year spell did little to erase that stain.
Deschamps’ first task was to restore France’s credibility. Fourteen years later, he walks away having delivered far more than most dared to expect, leaving behind a side that measures tournaments not by qualification, but by how far it goes.
The blueprint for Deschamps’ managerial philosophy was obvious to those who watched him play.
From Nantes, Marseille and Juventus to the French national team, Deschamps captained almost every side he represented. Leadership came naturally, but so did another conviction that would shape his managerial career: an organised team will almost always outperform a collection of outstanding individuals. Yes, talent mattered. But the collective mattered more.
As a player, Deschamps made his name as a defensive midfielder whose greatest gifts were discipline, intelligence and relentless industry. His job was simple — recover possession and move the ball to those capable of creating something extraordinary. Eric Cantona’s famous nickname for him, ‘the water-carrier’, was less than complimentary. But it perfectly captured Deschamps’ willingness to sacrifice personal glory for the team’s success.
Those same principles became the foundation of every French dressing room he commanded and helped him early on as he repaired a broken national side, both within the dressing room and beyond it.
relentless in their work rate, aggressive in their pressing, disciplined without the ball and exceptionally well organised. Superstars were encouraged, but never at the expense of team structure.
That pragmatism often made him an easy target for critics. What rarely received the same attention was his willingness to evolve. Over more than a decade in charge, Deschamps successfully navigated multiple generations of French talent — from Franck Ribery and Karim Benzema to Kylian Mbappe — adjusting his communication and leadership styles without ever compromising the standards he demanded.
The results speak for themselves. France reached the last four at the World Cup in three successive editions under Deschamps. It lifted the trophy in 2018, fell on penalties in the 2022 final and made a semifinal exit this year. In 2014, it was eliminated by eventual champion Germany in the quarterfinals. In England, a record like that would probably earn someone a knighthood — and then some.
“I’m extremely happy. I’m very proud of everything we’ve done to reach this stage and to win a World Cup, to take the French team to the highest level,” Deschamps told the press at this year’s quadrennial showpiece.
The irony is that his final chapter may have vindicated everything he had spent more than a decade preaching.
For years, Deschamps was criticised for being too cautious, too conservative, too reluctant to unleash France’s extraordinary attacking talent. In this World Cup, he defied his own patterns, loosened the reins and gave his star-studded side greater freedom. While that produced some of the tournament’s most attractive football, it would also be its undoing.
When Spain ended its campaign, it was not because France lacked flair. It was because it was overrun. It cried out for the very qualities that had long defined Deschamps’ best teams: discipline, composure and control. If anything, it served as a reminder that putting the handbrake on is not always a sign of fear. Sometimes, it is simply what wins football matches, especially in knockout games at the highest level.
Unlike many of football’s iconic players, Deschamps did not walk straight into elite managerial jobs on reputation alone. He earned his credentials by rebuilding clubs that needed rescuing. And he did it thrice.
AS Monaco came first. Appointed in 2001, he guided it to second place in Ligue 1 in only his second season, finishing just one point behind title-winning Olympique Lyonnais. He followed it with the League Cup triumph, famous Champions League victories over Real Madrid and Chelsea, and a run all the way to the final before Jose Mourinho’s FC Porto proved too strong.
Then came Juventus. Relegated to Serie B in the aftermath of the Calciopoli match-fixing scandal and burdened with a nine-point deduction, the Bianconeri needed stability as much as results. Deschamps delivered both, leading it straight back to Serie A as champion before resigning just a week after promotion following disagreements over transfer strategy.
His next revival came with Marseille, the club he had famously captained to Champions League glory as a player. In his first season, he ended an 18-year wait for the Ligue 1 title before adding three successive League Cups and two French Super Cups. Reawakening one of French football’s sleeping giants made him the obvious choice to succeed Blanc in 2012.
His record on the international stage is extraordinary. Five of the seven major tournaments in which France was eliminated under Deschamps ended with the team losing to the eventual champions. His tenure not only witnessed the makings of an enviable World Cup record, but also saw Les Bleus make the Euro final in 2016 and the semifinals in 2024.
And yet, despite everything he achieved, one question will linger. Could he have accomplished even more?
That says as much about the extraordinary depth of French talent as it does about the man who guided it. Deschamps inherited a stable overflowing with gifted footballers, but his greatest achievement was moulding them into a side that consistently functioned as something greater than the sum of its parts.
The debate over his legacy will not disappear anytime soon. Critics will argue that his caution prevented France from reaching even greater heights. His supporters will counter that his discipline transformed limitless potential into sustained excellence. The truth, as is so often the case with the finest managerial careers, probably lies somewhere in between.
Perhaps that is the paradox of Deschamps. The better France became under him, the more was expected of him. Winning the World Cup became the benchmark rather than the dream. Reaching the semifinals became routine instead of remarkable. All said and done, he leaves with France restored to where it belongs — among the game’s true heavyweights.
Another French legend, Zinedine Zidane, is widely tipped to be the man who follows him. Deschamps leaves behind a daunting assignment, though. His are far from impossible shoes to fill, but they are certainly not comfortable ones.

title: World Cup: Fulton feels underdog tag sits perfectly on India
content:
It’s been more than half a century that the Indian men’s hockey team has been anywhere near the World Cup podium. As Craig Fulton’s boys enter the final stretch of preparations for yet another shot at the medal, the coach is not only aware of the challenge ahead but also comfortable with the ‘underdog’ tag for his team.
“The ideal goal, of course, is to win. The realistic goal is we’ve been given a 5% chance of winning because we are ranked eighth. It’s perfectly set up for a World Cup. We go into it as underdogs, to be honest, and that’s a good place for us to be.
“The big block now is strength and conditioning because you need a certain amount of strength to get through seven games if you go all the way in the World Cup. And then we have a similar number of games in the Asian Games, so it’s 100% all-in, there are no easy games,” Fulton told The Hindu on Friday.
There will also be the Asian Games in two months with an Olympic ticket at stake. However, Fulton insisted the team wasn’t looking that far ahead, not even to the knockout stages of the World Cup yet. “The first goal is to get out of the pool in the top two, preferably in the number one position. We’re looking at all our tactical plans, all our opposition, our offensive, long corner, penalty corner type defence. We’re really trying to do a good job on what we’re going to be coming up against. And the guys are super motivated because everyone’s in a good place,” he said.
India’s first Pool D game will be against Wales on August 15, followed by England on 17 and Pakistan on 19 with the top two advancing to the quarterfinals. “We’re just looking at Wales as our number one game. They will be difficult opponents because they are the true underdogs in our pool, they have nothing to lose. There are Welsh players in the GB (Great Britain) programme so a lot of the style of play is very similar, strong, hard-running.
“England have a very experienced team and have got results against everyone. They had a fantastic Pro League. It’s nice to have played them twice before we play them in the pool. And Pakistan are Pakistan. They can score goals from nothing; at the same time, they can have a bad patch and you can score two-three goals as well. So, it’s an interesting pool. It’s up to us now to perform and get the results,” Fulton said.
The Indian squad will leave on July 31 for a team building and training camp in Switzerland with renowned mental-conditioning coach Paddy Upton. It will then have a training camp in Eindhoven and go to Amsterdam on August 8 and play warm-up games against Japan and Argentina.
“Everything we’re doing is building for one tournament with a second tournament in mind. It’s like having a goal, the World Cup, but we also have a goal through a goal, the Asian Games. All our training is geared around being physically, mentally and tactically sharp enough to cover both tournaments,” Fulton explained.
Asked about the pressure of expectations, Fulton admitted the title dream was alive but it was equally important to focus on the immediate task. “I think legacy always plays a part but this team wants to write its own piece of Indian history at the tournament. To perform and stand on the podium would be fantastic; to win it would be amazing. But the guys aren’t jumping too far ahead. It’s easy to dream and it is important to do so. But we’ve got to keep doing the hard work. We’ve got the last phase to go and the guys are excited about the opportunity”.

title: CWG 2026 medal table: Where does India stand after Jhandu's bronze on Day 2?
content:
India ended Day 2 of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow with its first medal of the campaign, while athletes delivered encouraging performances across para powerlifting, swimming, boxing and lawn bowls.
The day's biggest highlight came in para powerlifting, where Jhandu Kumar secured bronze in the men's heavyweight event to open India's medal tally. The Bihar lifter, who has overcome polio and financial struggles to reach the international stage, finished with 130.9 points after successful lifts of 181kg and 190kg. He narrowly missed a Commonwealth Games record with an unsuccessful 196kg attempt. Fellow Indian Sudhir placed sixth.
India came close to adding another medal in para powerlifting as Ashok Malik finished fourth in the men's lightweight event with 143.8 points, narrowly missing the podium. Paramjeet Kumar ended seventh.
In para swimming, Karthik Budigina narrowly missed a medal after finishing fourth in the men's 100m Freestyle S13 final with a time of 57.57 seconds. Teammate Imam Ali placed seventh after both Indians had progressed from the heats earlier in the day.

In swimming, Srihari Nataraj missed out on a place in the men's 50m backstroke final after finishing seventh in his semifinal.

title: Inside Ahmedabad's mega plan to host the 2030 CWG and 2036 Olympics
content:
Ahmedabad’s appetite for bold bets can be measured in acres. At a recent planning summit, Indian Olympic Association (IOA) senior vice-president Ajay Patel offered a striking comparison. “Paris used 400 acres for its 2024 Games. Ahmedabad has already acquired 1,000 acres.”
Officially, the city is preparing for the 2030 Commonwealth Games (CWG), the centenary edition of the event and India’s first since Delhi 2010. But nearly every major decision being taken today is being shaped by a larger ambition: positioning Ahmedabad as the host city for the 2036 Olympic Games. “The 2030 CWG is a dress rehearsal for the 2036 Summer Olympic Games,” Patel said. While the International Olympic Committee (IOC) is expected to take a final call on the 2036 host around 2029, Gujarat has already begun building as though the Olympics are coming.
A drive through Motera reflects the scale of that ambition. Construction cranes, excavators and scaffolding dominate the skyline as roads, sporting venues, transport systems and hotels take shape for an event still four years away.
At the heart of the transformation is the Rs 5,050-crore
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Sports Enclave (SVPSE), coming up around the Narendra Modi Stadium, the world’s largest cricket venue with a capacity of 1.32 lakh.
The stadium is set to host the opening and closing ceremonies of the CWG. The enclave will include a 12,000-seat aquatics centre, an 18,000-seat tennis centre and indoor arenas for basketball, gymnastics, volleyball, skateboarding, artistic swimming and sport climbing. To make way for the project, the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC) altered land-use plans across Sabarmati and Koteshwar, freeing nearly 14.5 lakh square metres.
Unlike several past multisport events where venues struggled to find a purpose after the Games, Gujarat says legacy planning has been built into the project from the outset. “We are adopting an asset utilisation model rather than a traditional ROI-based recovery approach,” Gujarat deputy chief minister Harsh Sanghavi, who led Ahmedabad’s CWG bid, told TOI . “The CWG infrastructure is a long-term investment in Ahmedabad’s transformation into an Olympic-ready global hub, not a sunk cost.” The venues will function as a year-round Games Plaza, hosting sporting events, concerts and exhibitions, with operational breakeven projected within five to seven years. A dedicated Infrastructure Legacy & Operations Trust (ILOT) is being created to manage the facilities at Motera and the Naranpura Sports Complex.
The sporting footprint extends well beyond Motera. Around 11km away, at Karai in Gandhinagar, a net-zero athletics stadium with a capacity of 50,000 and a worldclass shooting centre are under construction. The Rs 825-crore Naranpura Sports Complex is already operational, with facilities for badminton, squash, table tennis and Olympic-standard swimming.
Additional sports complexes have been completed in Vastral, while more are under construction in Gota, Ghuma, Naroda and Nikol. In all, 22 competition venues have been finalised across Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar. Sanghavi has set a firm deadline. “All major infrastructure will be ready by the end of 2029, leaving early 2030 for trial runs. By the time athletes and visitors arrive, Ahmedabad will be fully ready, with venues, transport and support systems functioning seamlessly.”
The makeover, however, extends far beyond stadiums. Ahmedabad’s vehicle population is growing by nearly nine per cent annually, significantly above the national average. To prevent congestion during the Games, planners have adopted what officials describe as a “30-minute city” model. The objective is simple: every athlete, official and spectator should be able to travel between venues, hotels and training centres within 30 minutes.
The existing 168km Bus Rapid Transit System (BRTS), which carries more than 2.2 lakh passengers a day, will be integrated with an expanding Metro network. A new northsouth Metro corridor and a parallel Neo Metro or light-rail system are each designed to carry around 70,000 passengers per hour in either direction.
A Rs 472-crore integrated ticketing platform will allow commuters to use a single QR code across the Metro, BRTS and a planned fleet of 3,000 electric buses. The road network is also being expanded. New arterial roads and northsouth and east-west corridors are being developed, while more than 100 roads are being widened. At the same time, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Airport is preparing for a sharp rise in traffic. A new integrated terminal is expected to double its annual capacity, while airports at Dholera, Vadodara and Surat could help handle the overflow during the Olympics.
Financing a project of this scale will require multiple funding streams. According to Gujarat’s Olympic bid estimates, the organising committee budget could range from Rs 18,557 crore to Rs 41,031 crore, while capital expenditure on infrastructure is projected at between Rs 16,060 crore and Rs 22,878 crore. The state plans to rely heavily on public-private partnerships, particularly for the Olympic Village and International Broadcast Centre. It is also proposing an ‘Adopt a Sport’ programme to encourage corporations to support athlete development and infrastructure through corporate social responsibility funding.
Officials cite Gujarat’s own sporting investment as evidence of its long-term commitment. The state’s sports budget has risen from Rs 2.5 crore in 2002 to Rs 521 crore today, while the Khel Mahakumbh programme now attracts more than seven million participants annually.
Accommodation remains one of the biggest challenges. The proposed Olympic Village, located within 5km of the Narendra Modi Stadium, will comprise 2,191 apartments capable of housing more than 17,500 athletes. The apartments are intended to be converted into premium residential housing.
The shortage of hotels presents an even tougher problem. Ahmedabad currently has just over 5,400 star-category rooms, while the long-term requirement for an Olympics is estimated at close to one lakh. The target is to increase capacity to 40,000 rooms before the 2030 Commonwealth Games through a new hotel policy offering capital subsidies. Parcels of land have already been earmarked for development, while neighbouring cities such as Vadodara and Mehsana are expected to absorb some of the additional demand.
The transformation also carries an ambitious sustainability agenda. Ahmedabad has committed to powering the proposed Olympics Games entirely through renewable energy, backed by upgraded battery-storage systems. Six million trees have already been planted against a target of 10 million, while every competition venue is expected to recycle and reuse all wastewater.
(With inputs from Kapil Dave and Parag Dave)

title: CWG: Jhandu Kumar wins India's first medal; day 2 brings mixed results in Glasgow
content:
India ended Day 2 of the Commonwealth Games with one medal and several encouraging performances across para powerlifting, swimming, boxing and lawn bowls, as athletes continued to progress in their respective events.
Jhandu Kumar wins India's first medalJhandu Kumar opened India's medal account by winning bronze in the men's heavyweight para powerlifting event.
The 28-year-old, who overcame polio, financial hardship and years of doing odd jobs before reaching the international stage, scored 130.9 points after successful lifts of 181kg and 190kg. He could not complete his final attempt of 196kg.
The other Indian in the event, Sudhir, finished sixth with 114.1 points.
Nigeria's Idris Riluwan won gold with 132.8 points, while Matthew Harding claimed silver with 131 points.
Ashok Malik finishes fourthIndia narrowly missed another medal in the men's lightweight para powerlifting event.
Ashok Malik finished fourth with 143.8 points, missing out on a podium finish.
England's Mark Swan won gold with 153.9 points. Nigeria's Roland Ezuruike (153.9) took silver, while Malaysia's Bonnie Bunyau Gustin (153.5) claimed bronze.
India's Paramjeet Kumar finished seventh with 135.6 points.
Karthik Budigina misses podium in para swimmingIndia came close to another medal when Karthik Budigina finished fourth in the men's 100m Freestyle S13 final.
Budigina clocked 57.57 seconds, while teammate Imam Ali finished seventh in 1:03.73.
South Africa's Nathan Hendricks won gold in 54.54 seconds. Scotland's Stephen Clegg took silver in 55.16 seconds and England's Matthew Redfern won bronze in 56.86 seconds.
The S13 category is for athletes with visual impairments.
Earlier in the day, both Budigina and Imam Ali had advanced to the final after all eight swimmers in the heats qualified. Budigina had finished third in the heats with a time of 57.10 seconds, while Imam Ali qualified with 1:05.32 seconds.
quarterfinalsIndian boxer Jadumani Singh made a winning start in the men's 55kg competition.
He defeated Scotland's Aaron Cullen by unanimous decision in the Round of 32 to move into the pre-quarterfinals, where he will face Pakistan's Sumama Rehman.
Srihari Nataraj misses finalSrihari Nataraj's campaign in the men's 50m backstroke ended in the semifinals.
The Indian swimmer finished seventh in his race with a time of 25.29 seconds and did not qualify for the final.
South Africa's Pieter Coetze qualified fastest in 24.29 seconds, ahead of compatriot Ruard van Renen (24.56) and England's Oliver Morgan (24.65).
Lawn bowls continue strong runIndia also enjoyed another successful day in lawn bowls.
In the men's singles, Putul Sonowal backed up his opening-day win over reigning world champion Ryan Bester of Canada with another hard-fought victory.
The Assam Police officer defeated Falkland Islands' Cecil Alexander in a tie-break after the match ended 1-1 in sets.
Sonowal recovered from a 3-4 deficit to win the opening set 7-5 before Alexander claimed the second set 8-6. The Indian then held his nerve in the tie-break to complete the win.

title: Argentina's own FA sends blunt message after viral World Cup final replay petition passes 100,000 signatures
content:
Argentina FA urges fans to accept Spain's World Cup victory as viral replay petition tops 100,000 signatures
The Argentine Football Association (AFA) has urged supporters to accept Spain's victory in the 2026 FIFA World Cup final after a fan-led petition demanding the match be replayed went viral in the days following Argentina's defeat in New Jersey.
Spain secured their second men's World Cup title with a 1-0 extra-time victory over defending champions Argentina after Ferran Torres scored the decisive goal in the 106th minute at the New York New Jersey Stadium. Luis de la Fuente's side controlled much of the contest, while Argentina struggled to create chances and finished the match with 10 players following Enzo Fernández's late dismissal.
The final has remained in the headlines ever since, not only because of the post-match altercation involving several Argentina players, but also because of growing conspiracy theories surrounding the officiating.
Replay petition gains traction online
petition launched on Change.org by Argentine supporter Gisela Sánchez has gathered more than 101,613 verified signatures, calling on FIFA to replay the World Cup final.
The petition alleges that Slovenian referee Slavko Vinčić delivered a "controversial and corrupt" performance and asks FIFA to investigate several decisions made during the match.
Its full description outlines concerns about the integrity of the officiating, claiming the final was overshadowed by alleged bias and questionable decisions.
It argues that fans expect matches to be decided by skill and effort rather than refereeing calls, and warns that failing to address such concerns could damage trust in the sport.
Argentina players react at the end of the World Cup final soccer match between Spain and Argentina in East Rutherford, N.J., near New York, Sunday, July 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Stephanie Scarbrough)
The petition also references videos circulating online that supporters believe show decisions favouring one side, and frames the issue as one that goes beyond Argentina, touching on the credibility of football globally.
“Therefore, we call upon FIFA to review these incidents with seriousness and transparency, and to consider replaying the final—this time without the influence of a corrupt referee.”
However, no evidence has been produced to substantiate allegations that the referee or FIFA acted improperly, and there is nothing to suggest the match was influenced by bribery or corruption.
Furthermore, petitions on Change.org carry no legal or sporting authority, and FIFA regulations provide for matches to be replayed only under extraordinary circumstances, not because of disagreement with refereeing decisions.
Amid the growing online campaign, Argentine Football Association president Claudio "Chiqui" Tapia publicly distanced the federation from the replay calls and urged supporters to accept the result.
FIFA president Gianni Infantino, left, and Argentine Soccer Association President Claudio Tapia clap before the World Cup round of 32 soccer match between Argentina and Cape Verde in Miami Gardens, Fla., Friday, July 3, 2026. (AP Photo/George Walker IV)
In a lengthy statement shared on Instagram, Tapia acknowledged Spain's superiority on the day while encouraging fans to continue supporting the national team despite the disappointment.
"We were unable to get past Spain," Tapia wrote.
"We couldn't beat Spain. They were superior, they won fair and square, and we have to acknowledge that."
He added that accepting defeat is part of elite sport.
"In sports, you also learn by accepting defeats with the same grace with which you celebrate victories."
While admitting that losing another World Cup final was painful, Tapia reminded supporters that the squad had once again reached the biggest stage in international football.
"Yes, we lost a final. But it's also true that this group had just brought immense joy to the country."
"Losing hurts. It hurts because we are competitive, because we are the most successful team in history, and because second place is never enough for us."
The AFA president also defended the commitment shown by Lionel Scaloni's squad throughout the tournament.
"Let's think about the sacrifice of these players, the coaching staff, and every person who worked for more than 50 days away from their families, with a single objective: to represent Argentina in the best way possible."
He concluded by warning supporters not to be influenced by misinformation.
"That's why you shouldn't be swayed by lies or by schemes that only seek to destabilise. Enough of trying to turn against those who have given so much to our football."
Scaloni also dismissed conspiracy theories
Tapia's comments echo those made earlier by Argentina head coach Lionel Scaloni, who also rejected suggestions that Vinčić's officiating decided the outcome of the final.
The Argentina manager acknowledged that Spain had simply been the better team on the night, despite disappointment over missing out on back-to-back World Cup titles.
Argentina head coach Lionel Scaloni reacts during the World Cup semifinal soccer match between England and Argentina in Atlanta, Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (AP Photo/Jacob Kupferman)
Ironically, Argentina themselves had faced repeated allegations of receiving favourable refereeing decisions earlier in the tournament. Among those to question FIFA's officiating was Egypt head coach Hossam Hassan, who claimed football's governing body wanted Lionel Messi and Argentina to remain in the competition for as long as possible.
In addition to the replay petition, another viral campaign circulated online calling for Argentina to be stripped of their place in future World Cups, reportedly attracting around 23 million signatures before being taken down. Like the replay petition, it holds no official weight but highlights the intense global reaction to the controversial final.

title: Argentina president Javier Milei breaks silence after 23 million sign petition demanding World Cup ban
content:
The fallout from Argentina's dramatic 2026 FIFA World Cup final defeat to Spain continues to intensify, with President Javier Milei launching a defiant social media response after an online petition calling for Argentina to be banned from future World Cups surpassed 23 million signatures.
However, attention quickly shifted away from the football after chaotic scenes erupted at the final whistle, prompting FIFA to open disciplinary proceedings into the conduct of several members of the Argentina delegation.
Petition surpasses 28 million signatures
"Argentina Out" campaign officially closed on 19 July 2026, immediately after the World Cup final, with exactly 23,316,108 verified signatures from supporters across roughly 170 countries. The petition narrowly missed the all-time Guinness World Record for the most-signed online petition, falling just short of the record 24.3 million signatures.
The campaign calls on FIFA to exclude Argentina from future World Cups, arguing that the team's conduct during and after the final damaged the image of the sport and calling for stronger action to protect fair play.
The petition emerged after a match in which Argentina accumulated repeated fouls, had midfielder Enzo Fernández sent off in stoppage time after receiving a second yellow card, and became involved in an ugly confrontation following Spain's victory.
Spain's Gavi, left, falls as he scuffles with Argentina's Leandro Paredes (5) and Thiago Almada during the World Cup final soccer match between Spain and Argentina in East Rutherford, N.J., near New York, Sunday, July 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)
Leandro Paredes was seen grabbing Spain defender Eric García by the throat before clashing with Gavi, while Nahuel Molina appeared to throw a punch toward Spain captain Rodri. FIFA has since launched an investigation into the incidents, with players, coaching staff and the Argentine Football Association potentially facing disciplinary sanctions.
Milei hits back with defiant social media posts
Rather than distancing himself from the growing controversy, Argentine President Javier Milei responded with a series of patriotic messages on Instagram defending the national team and criticising what he suggested was hostility toward Argentina.
"Do you have enemies? It means you once defended something. We defend Argentina."In another post, Milei claimed Argentina's global prominence was the reason behind the criticism.
"The problem with Argentina is that we stand out. We don't go unnoticed, people are jealous of us, and we're good at almost everything."He also shared an AI-generated image of himself tearing open his suit to reveal an Argentina shirt underneath, accompanied by the caption:
"Long live Argentina, damn it!"The posts were widely circulated as debate over Argentina's conduct continued both inside and outside the country.

The petition claims the final was influenced by "controversial and corrupt" officiating and asks FIFA to overturn the result.
However, no verified evidence has been presented to substantiate those allegations, and there is nothing to indicate that FIFA or Vinčić acted improperly during the match.
The Argentine Football Association has also sought to calm speculation surrounding replay demands, while AFA president Claudio "Chiqui" Tapia has urged supporters to accept Spain's victory.
Paredes remains unapologetic as FIFA investigation continues
The controversy has been compounded by comments from midfielder Leandro Paredes, who has come under intense scrutiny for his role in the post-match altercation.
In a social media message published after the final, Paredes expressed pride in Argentina's campaign but stopped short of apologising for his actions.
"Thank you, Argentina! I love you today and always," he wrote. "Today I write with a lot of pain in my heart because we couldn't give our country the joy it deserved, but with my chest filled with pride for giving everything we had and putting our flag at the top once again."
He added that it had been "an honour to be part of the best Argentina team in history."
Alongside Paredes, Nahuel Molina, Thiago Almada and assistant coach Roberto Ayala remain under FIFA investigation following the disturbances at MetLife Stadium.
Meanwhile, criticism has continued to grow beyond Argentina's borders. Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente recently described the scenes as "intolerable" and praised his players for maintaining their composure throughout the confrontation, while FIFA's disciplinary process remains ongoing as world football's governing body reviews referee reports and video footage from the final.

title: Australia World Cup star Cristian Volpato reportedly tests positive for cocaine after being stopped twice in one night
content:
Australia international Cristian Volpato has reportedly tested positive for cocaine after being stopped twice by police for speeding in Sydney on the same night, just days after representing the Socceroos at the 2026
FIFA World Cup.
The 22-year-old Sassuolo midfielder was first stopped late on Thursday night before being pulled over again less than two hours later, when police allege he returned a positive roadside drug test for cocaine.
The incident comes shortly after Volpato featured in Australia's World Cup campaign, having switched his international allegiance from Italy to Australia earlier this year before making three appearances at the tournament.
Stopped twice on the same night
According to reports, New South Wales Police said Volpato was first stopped at approximately 11:05 p.m. on Thursday while driving his BMW Coupe across Sydney's Anzac Bridge.
Police allege he was travelling between 86 km/h and 94 km/h in a 60 km/h zone.
A roadside breath test returned a negative result, and Volpato was issued with an infringement notice for speeding before being allowed to continue his journey.
However, at around 1:10 a.m. on Friday, officers stopped the midfielder again in the same area after allegedly recording his vehicle travelling at 109 km/h in the 60 km/h speed zone—almost double the legal limit.
Following the second stop, Volpato underwent a roadside drug test that allegedly produced a positive indication for cocaine.
Police subsequently collected a secondary oral fluid sample, which has been sent for further laboratory analysis to confirm the result.
His international driver's licence was also suspended for six months.
Australia's Cristian Volpato arrives at the stadium ahead the World Cup round of 32 soccer match between Australia and Egypt in Arlington, Texas, near Dallas, Friday, July 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Sam Hodde)
Authorities have not announced any criminal charges relating to the alleged drug result while awaiting confirmation from the secondary test.
Volpato's representatives have been approached for comment.
World Cup campaign came after international switch
The midfielder had only recently completed his first senior FIFA World Cup after making the decision to represent Australia instead of Italy.
Born and raised in Sydney, Volpato developed through the youth systems of Sydney United 58, Sydney FC and Western Sydney Wanderers before moving to Europe as a teenager.
He later progressed through Roma's academy before making his senior breakthrough in Serie A.
Sassuolo's Cristian Volpato controls the ball during the Serie A soccer match between AC Milan and Sassuolo at the San Siro stadium, in Milan, Italy, Dec. 30, 2023. (AP Photo/Antonio Calanni, File)
Sassuolo signed the attacking midfielder in 2023, where he has since scored seven goals across three seasons.
Before committing his future to Australia, Volpato had represented Italy at Under-19 and Under-20 level.
As recently as March, he admitted he was still waiting for a senior Italy call-up after progressing through the country's youth teams. However, with Italy ultimately failing to qualify for the 2026 World Cup, the midfielder switched allegiance and accepted Australia's invitation.
Volpato made three appearances during Australia's World Cup campaign in North America.
He was an unused substitute as the Socceroos opened the tournament with a 2-0 victory over Turkey before coming off the bench during a 2-0 defeat to the United States.
The 22-year-old then started Australia's goalless draw with Paraguay before also featuring in the Round of 32 meeting with Egypt.
Australia's tournament came to an end after losing to Egypt in a penalty shootout, with Volpato substituted before extra time.
The midfielder had been viewed as one of Australia's brightest emerging talents following his decision to represent the Socceroos, making the latest allegations an unwelcome development for both player and country.
